verses.zh: 因此我心战兢，从原处移动。
verses.en: At this also my heart poundsand leaps from its place.
verses.commentary:
37:1 This verse may be connected
to Job 37:33, "noise" of His presence.

- "trembles" – BDB 353, KB 350, Qal IMPERFECT,
cf. Exod. 19:16; 1 Sam. 14:15; Dan. 10:7

- "leaps" – BDB 684 I, KB 736, Qal IMPERFECT,
rare word found only here in Qal; note Hiphil in Hab. 3:6

This verse is obviously connected to Job 36:33. Job 36 and 37 comprise
one literary unit.

▣ "heart"
The MT has "my heart," referring to Elihu but the LXX has
"your," referring to Job. The thunderstorm described in the
last strophe of Job 36 was awesome and illustrated God's power. Often
thunder is used to describe God's voice (i.e., Job 37:4-5; Ps. 29:3-9).
Elihu mixes imagery when he describes the thunder as "roaring"
(i.e., lion), but it is powerful imagery.

verses.zh: 听啊，　神轰轰的声音是他口中所发的响声。
verses.en: Listen carefully[NOTE:1] to the thunder of his voice,to the rumbling[NOTE:2] that proceeds from his mouth.
notes: The imperative is followed by the infinitive absolute from the same root to express the intensity of the verb.
The word is the usual word for “to meditate; to murmur; to groan”; here it refers to the low building of the thunder as it rumbles in the sky. The thunder is the voice of God (see Ps 29).
verses.commentary:
37:2 "listen closely" This is the translation of a Qal
IMPERATIVE (PLURAL) and the
INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE of the same root (BDB 1033, KB 1570).
The book of Job does not use this grammatical feature of intensification often.

Notice the synonymous parallelism of Job 37:2 (cf. Job 36:29,30,32,33; 38:4,5,15,21).

- thunder. . .His voice

- rumbling. . .His mouth

The PLURAL points toward
Job and his three comforters, cf. Job 32:3,5; 34:2,10; 35:4.

verses.zh: 他发响声震遍天下，发电光闪到地极。
verses.en: Under the whole heaven he lets it go,even his lightning to the far corners[NOTE:1] of the earth.
notes: Heb “wings,” and then figuratively for the extremities of garments, of land, etc.
verses.commentary:
37:3 "the ends of the earth"
This is an expression of God's sovereign power over all creation (cf.
Job 28:24; 38:13). It is literally "the wings (BDB 489) of the
earth," meaning "corners" or "extremities."

37:5b This is the same thought as
Job 36:26b. Humans cannot comprehend God's power in the natural realm
(cf. Job 5:9; 11:7; 26:14), and much less in the spiritual realm (i.e.,
justice, fairness, mercy).

verses.zh: 随后人听见有雷声轰轰，大发威严，雷电接连不断。
verses.en: After that a voice roars;he thunders with an exalted voice,and he does not hold back his lightning bolts[NOTE:1] when his voice is heard.
notes: The verb simply has the pronominal suffix, “them.” The idea must be that when God brings in all the thunderings he does not hold back his lightning bolts either.

verses.zh: 神发出奇妙的雷声；他行大事，我们不能测透。
verses.en: God thunders with his voice in marvelous ways;[NOTE:1] he does great things beyond our understanding.[NOTE:2]
notes: The form is the Niphal participle, “wonders,” from the verb פָּלָא (palaʾ, “to be wonderful; to be extraordinary”). Some commentators suppress the repeated verb “thunders,” and supply other verbs like “shows” or “works,” enabling them to make “wonders” the object of the verb rather than leaving it in an adverbial role. But as H. H. Rowley (Job [NCBC], 236) notes, no change is needed, for one is not surprised to find repetition in Elihu’s words.
Heb “and we do not know.”

verses.zh: 他对雪说：要降在地上；对大雨和暴雨也是这样说。
verses.en: For to the snow he says, ‘Fall[NOTE:1] to earth,’and to the torrential rains,[NOTE:2] ‘Pour down.’[NOTE:3]
notes: The verb actually means “be” (found here in the Aramaic form). The verb “to be” can mean “to happen, to fall, to come about.”

Heb “and [to the] shower of rain and shower of rains, be strong.” Many think the repetition grew up by variant readings; several Hebrew mss delete the second pair, and so many editors do. But the repetition may have served to stress the idea that the rains were heavy.
Heb “Be strong.”
verses.commentary:
37:6 "Fall on the earth"
This is God's voice speaking (cf. Job 37:4-5) to a snow storm (i.e.,
personification, BDB 216, KB 241, Qal IMPERATIVE).
This is beautiful imagery of the God of creation intimately involved in His creation.

Both NASB ("be strong") and NJB ("now rain hard")
see the last line as also an IMPERATIVAL
use (lit. a NOUN, "his
strength," BDB 738). They get this translation by changing the
vowels.

37:7a The VERB "seals" (BDB 367,
KB 364, Qal IMPERFECT)
is used in a unique sense of "knowing God's ways in weather."
Job 37:7-8 expresses the natural revelation (i.e., Ps. 19:1-6) that both
humans and animals understand natural cycles of weather and how to
prepare (i.e., shut themselves inside).

The LXX translates this line as "so that every human being may know
his own weakness," but the Peshitta is much like the NASB, "all
humans recognize God's power in the natural order."

It is possible to see the root, "know," as being "rest."
This would form a better parallelism. At the approach of a powerful
storm front, both humans and animals take shelter until it passes by.

verses.zh: 他封住各人的手，叫所造的万人都晓得他的作为。
verses.en: He causes everyone to stop working,[NOTE:1] so that all people[NOTE:2] may know[NOTE:3] his work.
notes: Heb “by the hand of every man he seals.” This line is intended to mean that with the heavy rains God suspends all agricultural activity.

This reading involves a change in the text, for in MT “men” is in the construct. It would be translated “all men whom he made” (i.e., “all men of his making”). This is the translation followed by the NIV and NRSV. Olshausen suggested that the word should have been אֲנָשִׁים (ʾanashim) with the final ם (mem) being lost to haplography.

D. W. Thomas suggested a meaning of “rest” for the verb, based on Arabic. He then reads אֱנוֹשׁ (ʾenosh) for man, and supplies a ם (mem) to “his work” to get “that every man might rest from his work [in the fields].”

verses.zh: 百兽进入穴中，卧在洞内。
verses.en: The wild animals go to their lairs,and in their dens they remain.

verses.zh: 暴风出于南宫；寒冷出于北方。
verses.en: A tempest blows out from its chamber,icy cold from the driving winds.[NOTE:1]
notes: The “driving winds” reflects the Hebrew “from the scatterers.” This refers to the north winds that bring the cold air and the ice and snow and hard rains.
verses.commentary:
37:9

NASB, TEV
"south"

NKJV
"the chamber of the south"

NRSV, JPSOA, LXX
"the Mansion of the South"

REB
"its prison"

Peshitta
"the inner chambers"

The MT has "from its chamber" (BDB 293, KB 293). This word can
denote a type of storeroom (Prov. 24:4).

- in Job 9:9 it stored the constellations (cf. Job 38:32a)

- here it stores the cold wind (cf. Job 38:22; Ps. 135:7c)

▣

NASB
"the north the cold"

NKJV, NRSV
"cold from the scattering winds of the north"

TEV
"the biting cold from the north"

NJB
"the north winds usher in the cold"

JPSOA
"the cold from the constellations"

REB
"the rain winds bring bitter cold"

LXX
"cold from the peaks"

Peshitta
"cold out of the downpour"

The MT has "from scattering winds cold." The VERB
"scatter" (BDB 279, KB 280, Piel ACTIVE PARTICIPLE)
in Piel normally means "to scatter people." In Job 18:15 the Pual
is used of destruction, but here in a nature context, "strong, cold, northern winds"
seems best (KB 567, cf. I Enoch 76:10).

verses.zh: 神嘘气成冰；宽阔之水也都凝结。
verses.en: The breath of God produces ice,and the breadth of the waters freeze solid.
verses.commentary:
37:10 This is anthropomorphic
language about God's creation of ice (cf. Job 38:29).

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD DESCRIBED AS HUMAN (ANTHROPOMORPHISM)

verses.zh: 他使密云盛满水气，布散电光之云；
verses.en: He loads the clouds with moisture;[NOTE:1] he scatters his lightning through the clouds.
notes: The word “moisture” is drawn from רִי (ri) as a contraction for רְוִי (revi). Others emended the text to get “hail” (NAB) or “lightning,” or even “the Creator.” For these, see the various commentaries. There is no reason to change the reading of the MT when it makes perfectly good sense.
verses.commentary:
37:11 "moisture" This
term (BDB 924, KB 1223) occurs only here and is assumed to be related to
"watered," but AB (p. 243) thinks it is parallel to "light"
or "lightning" (BDB 21). This is possible by taking the
PREPOSITION "b" as the
first letter of another root (i.e., "hail" or "lightning").

▣

NASB, NRSV, JPSOA, NET
"loads"

NKJV
"saturates"

NJB
"weighs"

REB
"hurls lightning"

Peshitta
"stretched"

This VERB (BDB 382, KB
379, Hiphil IMPERFECT)
is found only here. BDB says it means "to toil" or "to be
burdened" from an Aramaic root, "to toil," and/or an
Arabic root, "to cast" or "to throw" (i.e.,
lightning, NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 384). The same root was used in later
Hebrew for "burden" or "load" (i.e., Deut. 1:12;
Isa. 1:14).

verses.zh: 这云是藉他的指引游行旋转，得以在全地面上行他一切所吩咐的，
verses.en: The clouds[NOTE:1] go round in circles,wheeling about according to his plans,to carry out[NOTE:2] all that he commands themover the face of the whole inhabited world.
notes: The words “the clouds” are supplied from v. 11; the sentence itself actually starts: “and it goes round,” referring to the cloud.
Heb “that it may do.”
verses.commentary:
37:12-13 God controls nature for
His purposes (i.e., "He causes it to happen," Job 37:13b).

- judgment ("the rod," BDB 986, cf. Job 21:9)

- promised blessing (hesed, BDB 338, see

SPECIAL TOPIC: LOVINGKINDNESS

37:12c "on the face of the inhabited earth" The MT has "on
the face of the world of the earth." This unusual phrase occurs only here and Prov. 8:31.

verses.zh: 或为责罚，或为润地，或为施行慈爱。
verses.en: Whether it is for punishment,[NOTE:1]or for his land,or for mercy, he causes it to find its mark.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “rod,” i.e., a rod used for punishment.

This is interpretive; Heb “he makes find it.” The lightning could be what is intended here, for it finds its mark. But R. Gordis (Job, 429) suggests man is the subject—let him find what it is for, i.e., the fate appropriate for him.

verses.zh: 约伯啊，你要留心听，要站立思想　神奇妙的作为。
verses.en: “Pay attention to this, Job!Stand still and consider the wonders God works.
verses.commentary:
37:14 This verse, which starts a
new strophe, Job 37:14-20, has three
IMPERATIVES.

- listen – BDB 24, KB 27, Hiphil

- stand – BDB 763, KB 840, Qal

- consider – BDB 106, KB 122, Hithpolel

Elihu has often used IMPERATIVES
to begin his monologs (cf. Job 32:10; 33:1,31,33; 34:2,10,16; 36:2;
37:2; JUSSIVE in 32:20).
In this strophe Elihu is addressing Job directly.

Notice, here the subject of Elihu's comments will be "the wonders
of God" (BDB 810 CONSTRUCT
BDB 42).

For "wondrous" see

SPECIAL TOPIC: WONDERFUL THINGS.

verses.zh: 神如何吩咐这些，如何使云中的电光照耀，你知道吗？
verses.en: Do you know how God commands them,[NOTE:1] how he makes lightning flash in his storm cloud?[NOTE:2]
notes: The verb is בְּשׂוּם (besum, from שִׂים [sim, “set”]), so the idea is how God lays [or sets] [a command] for them. The suffix is proleptic, to be clarified in the second colon.
Dhorme reads this “and how his stormcloud makes lightning to flash forth?”
verses.commentary:
37:15 "Do you know"
This phrase is repeated twice (Job 37:15,16). These rhetorical questions
are similar to God's questioning of Job in Job 38:1-42:6. This is
literary foreshadowing (see Jerome Biblical Commentary, p. 530).
Job does not know, no human knows! God is above mankind (cf. Isa.
55:9-11). Without revelation mankind remains ignorant.

37:16a

NASB
"layers"

NKJV, NRSV, NJB, Peshitta, NET
"balance"

TEV
"float"

JPSOA
"expanse"

REB
"hang poised"

LXX
"the division"

The MT has "swaying," "poising" (BDB 814, KB 618),
which is found only here in the OT but possibly a similar root in Job
36:29 is the key to understanding.

- פלש – BDB 814, "to sway"

- פרש – BDB 831, "to spread out"

▣ "of one perfect in knowledge" In Job 36:4 this
descriptive phrase referred to Elihu but here obviously of God.

verses.zh: 云彩如何浮于空中，那知识全备者奇妙的作为，你知道吗？
verses.en: Do you know about the balancing[NOTE:1] of the clouds,that wondrous activity of him who is perfect in knowledge?
notes: As indicated by HALOT 618 s.v. מִפְלָשׂ, the concept of “balancing” probably refers to “floating” or “suspension” (cf. NIV’s “how the clouds hang poised” and J. E. Hartley, Job [NICOT], 481-82, n. 2).

verses.zh: 南风使地寂静，你的衣服就如火热，你知道吗？
verses.en: You, whose garments are hotwhen the earth is still because of the south wind,
verses.commentary:
37:17 "You whose garments are hot"
The "you" is SINGULAR
and may refer to Job's agitation at God's lack of response to his court
case against Him (cf. Job 37:19; 13:18; 23:4; 31:35; 32:14; 33:5).

In Job 37:18 the question to Job is sarcastic, as is the Hiphil
IMPERATIVE, "teach us" in Job 37:19.

Job has accused God of overpowering him, terrifying him so that he
cannot, or will not, bring his case of innocense before Him.

verses.zh: 你岂能与　神同铺穹苍吗？这穹苍坚硬，如同铸成的镜子。
verses.en: will you, with him, spread out[NOTE:1] the clouds,solid as a mirror of molten metal?
notes: The verb means “to beat out; to flatten,” and the analogy in the next line will use molten metal. From this verb is derived the word for the “firmament” in Gen 1:6-8, that canopy-like pressure area separating water above and water below.
verses.commentary:
37:18 "spread out the skies"
It is possible to see this verse as referring to

- God's creation of the atmosphere (see note below)

- God sending the south wind (Job 37:17) to clear the sky of clouds (i.e., no shade)

▣ "a molten mirror"
Mirrors in the ANE were made from polished bronze (i.e., Exod. 38:8).
The parallel between lines a and b is related to the ancient view that
the sky was also a dome of bronze (or animal skin, cf. Job 9:8; Isa.
40:22; 45:12; Zech. 12:1). Deuteronomy 28:23 uses this same imagery for
God's judgment of Israel (i.e., no rain).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE CIRCLE OF THE EARTH

verses.zh: 我们愚昧不能陈说；请你指教我们该对他说甚么话。
verses.en: Tell us what we should[NOTE:1] say to him.We cannot prepare a case[NOTE:2] because of the darkness.
notes: The imperfect verb here carries the obligatory nuance, “what we should say?”
The verb means “to arrange; to set in order.” From the context the idea of a legal case is included.

verses.zh: 人岂可说：我愿与他说话？岂有人自愿灭亡吗？
verses.en: Should he be informed that I want[NOTE:1] to speak?If a man speaks, surely he will be swallowed up!
notes: This imperfect works well as a desiderative imperfect.

verses.zh: 现在有云遮蔽，人不得见穹苍的光亮；但风吹过，天又发晴。
verses.en: But now, the sun[NOTE:1] cannot be looked at[NOTE:2]—it is bright in the skies—after a wind passed and swept the clouds away.[NOTE:3]
notes: The light here must refer to the sun in the skies that had been veiled by the storm. Then, when the winds blew the clouds away, it could not be looked at because it was so dazzling. Elihu’s analogy will be that God is the same—in his glory one cannot look at him or challenge him.
The verb has an indefinite subject, and so should be a passive here.

Heb “and cleaned them.” The referent is the clouds (v. 18), which has been supplied in the translation for clarity. There is another way of reading this verse: the word translated “bright” means “dark; obscured” in Syriac. In this interpretation the first line would mean that they could not see the sun because it was darkened by the clouds, but then the wind came and blew the clouds away. Dhorme, Gray, and several others take it this way, as does the NAB.
verses.commentary:
37:21-24 The nature imagery of a
powerful storm continues. Humans are awed at God's power. Not only in
the created order (Job 37:21-22) but also in justice (Job 37:23-24). Job
should be ashamed of questioning God's power and justice. Job is not
"wise of heart" (implied in Job 37:24).

verses.zh: 金光出于北方，在　神那里有可怕的威严。
verses.en: From the north he comes in golden splendor;[NOTE:1] around God is awesome majesty.
notes: The MT has “out of the north comes gold.” Left in that sense the line seems irrelevant. The translation “golden splendor” (with RV, RSV, NRSV, NIV) depends upon the context of theophany. Others suggest “golden rays” (Dhorme), the aurora borealis (Graetz, Gray), or some mythological allusion (Pope), such as Baal’s palace. Golden rays or splendor is what is intended, although the reference is not to a natural phenomenon—it is something that would suggest the glory of God.
verses.commentary:
37:22 AB (pp. 245-246) links this
text to the Ugaritic Ba'al poems, which describe a golden palace
on top of Mt. Zaphon (the mountain in the north, cf. Ps. 48:1-3; Isa.
14:13; NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 836; Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel,
vol. 2, pp. 279-281).

verses.zh: 论到全能者，我们不能测度；他大有能力，有公平和大义，必不苦待人。
verses.en: As for the Almighty,[NOTE:1] we cannot attain to him!He is great in power,but justice[NOTE:2] and abundant righteousness he does not oppress.
notes: The name “Almighty” is here a casus pendens, isolating the name at the front of the sentence and resuming it with a pronoun.

The MT places the major disjunctive accent (the atnach) under “power,” indicating that “and justice” starts the second half of the verse as a disjunctive clause (with ESV, NASB, NIV, NLT). Ignoring the Masoretic accent, NRSV has “he is great in power and justice.”
verses.commentary:
37:23 "The Almighty"
See
SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADDAI

▣ "we cannot find Him"
Elihu is reacting to Job's previous words about God being hidden from
him (possibly Job 11:7-8; 13:24).

▣ "He will not do violence to justice and abundant
righteousness" This is also a reaction
to Job's words in Job 9:20-24; 10:3; 12:6.

verses.zh: 所以，人敬畏他；凡自以为心中有智慧的人，他都不顾念。
verses.en: Therefore people fear him,for he does not regard all the wise in heart.”[NOTE:1]
notes: The phrase “wise of heart” was used in Job 9:4 in a negative sense.

37:24 "fear" See

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are
responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You,
the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this
section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

- What is the purpose of Elihu's nature imagery?

- Why is Job 37:7 so hard to interpret?

- Job 37:13 lists two purposes of God's control of nature. What are they? How do they relate to Job?

- Is Job 37:17a literal (i.e., hot weather) or figurative (i.e., Job's anger at God)?

- Does Job 37:19 refer to Job's legal case? Why or why not?

- What does "out of the north comes golden splendor" in Job 37:22a mean?

- Explain "we cannot find Him" in Job 37:23a.

- Is Job 37:24 a typical wisdom close or a direct reference to Job?

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- Job 37 continues an emphasis on God's exalted power in the
natural realm (cf. Job 36:22-23,24-37:24).

- It is even possible to denote the seasons of the ANE.

- autumn (the rainy season, cf. Job 36:37-33; 37:1-5)

- winter (snow and ice, cf. Job 37:6-13)

- summer (hot, south wind, cf. Job 37:14-22)

- Much of Elihu's nature imagery is a foreshadowing of God's response to
Job in Job 38:1-42:6.

- Neither Job nor God responded to Elihu's speeches! Is this a sign that

- he won the argument

- God accepted his words because He does not mention him in His
rejection of Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar

- he is simply ignored

- he was a literary way of introducing God's words to Job
